card.name: Mak Sa'moa
card.tagline: An informal Rotuman dance of Samoan lineage characterized by intricate hand and footwork.
card.profile: Mak Sa'moa is an informal dance form from the island of Rotuma, derived from Samoan movement traditions. Meaning 'Samoan dance' in the Rotuman language, it features distinct hand movements between male and female dancers alongside feet shuffling and twisting in and out, reflecting patterns seen in the Siva Samoa. Favored particularly by older generations of Rotuman people for its measured, slower pace, the dance forms a core element of social gatherings during the seasonal av' mane'a festivities known as the fara.
card.insight: Though long regarded by Rotumans as their own heritage, contact with 19th-century missionaries revealed Mak Sa'moa was originally inherited from early Samoan ancestors like Raho.
card.profile_long:
Mak Sa'moa is an informal Rotuman dance tradition whose name translates directly as 'Samoan dance' in the Rotuman language. For generations, the dance was integrated into local custom and held to be an original Rotuman tradition. It was only after contact with Christian missionaries—specifically representatives from the London Missionary Society and the Methodist Church of Fiji and Rotuma—that Rotumans recognized the form had been inherited from early Samoan ancestors, including the legendary founder Raho, to whom islanders attribute the founding of Rotuma.

The dance movement draws directly from the movement repertoire of the Siva Samoa. Dancers execute a characteristic footwork pattern involving the inward and outward shuffling and twisting of the feet. Hand movements are performed in an interactive style between men and women, establishing a rhythmic visual counterpoint to the leg work. Compared to other regional forms, Mak Sa'moa is characterized by a measured and generally slower pace.

In contemporary practice, Mak Sa'moa is particularly popular among older generations of Rotuman people. Older dancers appreciate its unhurried tempo and the traditional style of its music and lyrics, which stand in contrast to faster borrowing styles like Mak Rarotoga, whose accelerated rhythms emulate Tahitian otea and Rarotongan tamure dances. Mak Sa'moa remains a fixture during the av' mane'a season, performed prominently during the community festivities of the Rotuman fara.

sections.origins_and_history: Mak Sa'moa, which translates to 'Samoan dance' in Rotuman, originated from Samoan movement styles introduced by early ancestors such as Raho, whom Rotumans venerate as the founder of their islands. Although long performed as a customary Rotuman dance, islanders only realized its explicit Samoan origin following interaction with London Missionary Society and Methodist Church missionaries in the modern era.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed informally with interactions between male and female partners. The core movement mechanics rely on hand movements exchanged between man and woman, accompanied by footwork where dancers shuffle and twist their feet inward and outward, recalling the movement patterns of the Siva Samoa. The overall execution follows a deliberate, generally slower pace.

sections.occasions_and_meaning: Mak Sa'moa is commonly performed during the av' mane'a season as part of the Rotuman fara festivities. It serves as a valued social expression, particularly among older generations who cherish its links to ancestral history and measured musical pace.
sections.notable_figures: Raho, the legendary founder of Rotuma, is cited in oral tradition as one of the early Samoan ancestors from whom the dance form was derived.
sections.lineage: Mak Sa'moa derives from early Samoan dance traditions, specifically carrying movement patterns shared with the Samoan Siva Samoa, adapted into Rotuman informal social dance.
